newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes one commissioner per country.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes one commissioner per country.

text.p: Each European Union country should be allowed just one member on the European Commission so the body does not become too unwieldy to operate in an EU of 20 or members, the Commission said on Friday.

Setting out a plan for reforming itself before the Union takes in new members and adopts a single currency, the EU executive also proposed creating a foreign affairs vice president and giving only about half its members portfolios.

The question of how big the Commission should be is a sensitive one, with some smaller countries fearing they will be steamrolled into giving up their commissioners as the EU grows to take in members from central and Eastern Europe.
The Commission's proposals, which will be submitted to the inter-governmental conference (IGC), would force the big countries in the 15-member EU to give up one commissioner.

Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain now have two representatives each on the 20-member Commission. The Commission said in a policy paper that its one-member-per-country plan should apply until the EU hits 20 members.
It said the system should then be reassessed, but it does not say how.
The Commission also proposed naming three vice presidents -- one for external relations, one for economic affairs and a third for internal policies and "the interest of citizens".
"It is quite obvious thaqt there is a need for the Commission to have in external relations a greater coherence," Jim Cloos, chief aide to Commission President Jacques Santer, told reporters.

The vice president would be the Commission's "alter ego" in deadling with EU foreign affairs ministers, he said. At least four members of the present Commission have responsibility for external relations dossiers.

The Commission said 10 or 12 of its members should be given specific portfolios, while the others should be given special missions or "support tasks". The paper does not elaborate what those could be.

The executive also proposed that its president be named by EU government leaders and approved by the European Parliament. The president would then agree jointly with national governments on the other members.

Possibly choosing from a list drawn up by governments, the president would try to make a good match between candidates and portolios and ensure a "balanced" number of men and women, the Commissions said.
Commissioners are now named by their governments and the parliament decides whether to confirm the entire body as a bloc.
The Commission said its proposal would require changes in EU treaty articles 157, 158 and 161.
